sections.name: Inventory and variance

lines.label: In short
lines.text: What you used against what you sold.

know: Variance = what the POS sold − usage.

read.bigIdea: Pour cost tells you if beer earns its place.
read.where: **Pour cost** is what the beer costs ÷ what it sells for; for the whole bar, **usage ÷ sales**. Backbar (bar inventory software) gives common targets: **draft about 20%**, **bottles about 25%**, spirits about 15%. BevSpot’s customer data put the median beer pour cost at **24%**, the best bars at 20% or lower. These are **rules of thumb**: our real targets are the GM’s call.
read.mixup: A low pour cost isn’t always good. Price beer too high and it doesn’t sell.

keyPoints.line: keg cost ÷ pour cost = keg revenue.

read.where: Backbar’s method: **pours per keg** = keg ounces ÷ liquid ounces per pour. **Keg revenue** = keg cost ÷ target pour cost. **Price** = keg revenue ÷ pours, rounded up. Their example: a **$120** half barrel at **20%** needs **$600**; 1,984 oz ÷ **14.5 oz** (a 16 oz glass with about 1.5 oz of foam) is about **136 pours**; $600 ÷ 136 ≈ **$4.41**, so **$4.50**.
read.mixup: Don’t divide by 16 for a pint. The foam isn’t all beer, so the liquid pour is less.

read.where: Find the **unit cost**: a **$25.99** case of 24 is about **$1.08** a bottle. Divide by the **target**: $1.08 ÷ 0.25 ≈ **$4.32**, rounded to **$4.50**. Some bars use a markup instead (2–3× cost). **Packaged** beer has little spillage, so its cost percentage stays steadier than draft.
read.mixup: Use the percent as a decimal: divide by 0.25, not 25.

keyPoints.line: of head is right, and profitable.

read.bigIdea: Every lost ounce raises the real cost.
read.where: A **1-inch head** is the right pour: foam is 25–33% beer, and filling to the rim is over-pouring. Siebel Institute: losing **1 oz per pint** is **6.25%** of the keg; at a $4 pint, that’s about **$31 a keg**. Each **line clean** dumps the beer in the line: 50 ft of 3/8-inch line holds about **37 oz**, more than two pints. An open faucet with no glass runs about **2 oz a second** down the drain.
read.mixup: Topping off a foamy pour by letting it run over the glass pours money into the drain.

keyPoints.line: kegs on a scale, not by kicking.

read.where: **Usage** = beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory (at cost). **Variance** = the cost of what the POS says you sold − usage; BevSpot’s example: **$10,000** used but only **$8,000** sold is a **−20%** variance. Causes: miscounts, **over-pouring**, comps, theft. Counting kegs by “touch and guess” is the least accurate; **weighing** on a keg scale (minus the empty keg) is better.
read.mixup: A big variance isn’t always theft. Start with the count and the pour.

sources: BevSpot blog (bar inventory software); Backbar Academy (bar inventory software); Siebel Institute, “How much does wasting draught beer cost?”; Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
